content:
Hi everyone!

I’m excited to announce a project I’ve been working on for the past few months as part of my PhD under my advisor @Jarod Alper : a verified implementation of Brown–Traub’s subresultant polynomial remainder sequence algorithm in Lean. The algorithm is essentially a modification of the Euclidean algorithm applied to polynomials over arbitrary integral domains that helps prevent coefficient explosion. The algorithm itself is easy to implement - proving correctness is where the challenge lies.

So, the goal is to formalize both the underlying theory of subresultants and the correctness of an efficient PRS-based algorithm for computing them. Resultants appear as a special case. I was motivated to work on this project by two observations that came up in a previous "zulip thread":

  • Efficiently computing subresultants seems to be one of the main roadblocks to implementing a potential cylindrical algebraic decomposition tactic.

  • Efficiently computing resultants would help support a computable implementation of algebraic numbers, which I think would be very cool to have.

This project is currently a work in progress, but I wanted to share the intended scope and also check whether anyone else is working on something similar.

The first part of the project will be developed in mathlib’s usual Polynomial type. I hope to eventually release this as one or more PRs to mathlib. The intended pieces are:

  1. A formalization of subresultants as determinant polynomials of certain coefficient matrices associated to two input polynomials.

  2. A theory of polynomial remainder sequences, including a proof that the normalized pseudo-division PRS computes the subresultants of the original pair of polynomials.

The mathematics is conceptually straightforward, but writing down the formal statements is quite difficult because many arguments rely on visually reasoning about the shape of certain matrices and their block decompositions. Based on my current experimental attempt, I expect this part of the project to be fairly large, perhaps on the order of 10k lines of code.

Disclaimer: I plan to use AI-assisted development while building this formalization. I know this raises review concerns, so I would be very interested in advice about how best to ease the process. I'm happy to make small, incremental PRs. 

Since mathlib’s Polynomial type is noncomputable, the executable implementation will probably live separately. My current plan is to use the external CompPoly library, which provides a computable polynomial representation together with an equivalence to mathlib polynomials. After implementing the executable algorithm there, I would like to prove that it agrees with the mathlib specification. This part may be better suited to live in the CompPoly library or in a companion project rather than directly in mathlib.

At the moment, the project consists of a messy experimental formalization where I worked through several design issues. I am now planning to restart with a cleaner architecture: first the mathlib theory, then the PRS correctness theorem, and only afterward the executable layer.

Please let me know if you have feedback, suggestions, or concerns about this plan. If anyone else is working on related formalizations of resultants, subresultants, PRS algorithms, CAD infrastructure, or computable algebraic numbers, I would be very happy to coordinate!

Thanks,
Dhruv Bhatia

This topic was moved here from #mathlib4 > Project Announcement: Computable Resultants in Lean by Filippo A. E. Nuccio.

Efficiently computing subresultants seems to be one of the main roadblocks to implementing a potential cylindrical algebraic decomposition tactic.

It's worth noting that (AFAIK) you shouldn't need to a full formal Lean implementation of Brown–Traub’s algorithm in order to implement this tactic. Your tactic can just be a standard implementation of the algorithm, and as long as it produces correct proof terms it should be usable.

Thanks for helping get this post moved to the appropriate place .

It sounds like you're announcing you plan to write 10k lines with an LLM and PR it to mathlib, which is worrying.

I'm definitely wary of the amount of code my current implementation is using - switching to an LLM made that more manageable, but maybe I'm losing sight and missing some things.

It's worth noting that (AFAIK) you shouldn't need to a full formal Lean implementation of Brown–Traub’s algorithm in order to implement this tactic. Your tactic can just be a standard implementation of the algorithm, and as long as it produces correct proof terms it should be usable.

My understanding is there are ways to certify that a given polynomial is the resultant up to scaling. I'm not so sure for the subresultant, which would be needed for finding the degree of the gcd. Can those proof terms also be generated?

I'm also concerned about exact division, and how one would prove that the algorithm doesn't take us outside the coefficient ring. Probably this can be certified as well?

I'll look more into this, thanks. It would definitely make the project a lot easier/shorter.
